doc.title: Jimmy Lewis interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: King Curtis, session work on Fender bass, and how Hair began
summary: After seven years with King Curtis, Lewis becomes a busy Fender bass session player and writes bass lines for Galt MacDermot's music, leading to Hair.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Yeah. I worked with King Curtis for seven years. Formed a solid band, everything. But then I would go downtown and they’d call me for a record date and all. So I had to start playing the Fender bass. I had a different style from all the guys on the Fender bass — my own creation. But it worked out nice for me. So the first week I went down I think I made about three sessions, and I got seven hundred and something dollars. So I said now wait a minute — there’s money in this thing. I wonder if I can keep it going. So then I gave King Curtis my notice. Because he kept calling me you know. And this guy named Ray Burns, he saw me down there. And he says, “Jimmy, I heard you on one of these records down here, you’re playing the Fender.” I says, “yeah.” He said, “well you got a pencil and paper?” I said, “yeah.” I kept a little book, you know. He said “I’ve got 17 dates for you,” 17 recording dates. I put that down, and I made those dates, and you know you had to go to the union to pick up your check. I’m standing at the window picking up my check and one of the guys turned over and looked mad, I was picking up so many. And so after that I started — there was this play on Broadway called “Hair.” They came along. So there was a guy named Galt McDermott, he had a lot of music that he had been trying to get people to listen to, but he didn’t know what to do with it. He told me, “I don’t know what to do with this.” He said, “I can’t think of no bass lines,” he said, “I thought of a melody, but I can’t think of no lines.” I said, “I’ll tell you, play it. I’ll put some lines to it.” So I put some lines to the music and I think he put it on a record called, a company called Kilimanjaro I think he said it was, out of somewhere in Canada. And the thing, he called me two weeks later and he said, “Jimmy.” He said, “the thing is selling. People are listening to my music.” I said, “Yeah?” He said, “Could you come down to do one more date?” So I went down and when I got there that’s when he told me about “Hair.” He said, “Will you try to do that?” He said, “they got a lot of music.” I said, “well we’ll give it a try, I don’t know.” I went down there and went to the Shakespeare House down on, I forgot, anyway, we got down there and that’s where we rehearsed you know. Put the music down. I started, so he had a lot of chords down. So I took it and built bass lines from the chords you know. So I kept doing that and they had about thirty-some tunes. And so I looked at the guys and looked at the actors act out there, and I said now this kind of line would fit what they’re doing. You know so I’d look at that and then I put the thing together, and so we had a piano player named Neal Tate.
